questions.q: An order service saves the order and then calls `$bus->dispatch(new OrderPlaced(...))` (RabbitMQ transport). When does this cause trouble?
questions.hint: What if something happens between the commit and the dispatch?

options.text: If the server crashes after the commit but before the dispatch, the event is lost
options.why: The database and the broker are not in one transaction. In the gap between them, the fact and the news come apart.

options.text: RabbitMQ is slow, so saving the order fails
options.why: The dispatch happens after the commit, so a slow broker doesn't block saving. The problem is losing events, not speed.

options.text: Messenger serializes the same message twice
options.why: That doesn't happen; the real problem is that the two systems are not in one transaction.

options.text: There is no problem, because Messenger is itself atomic
options.why: The broker outside Messenger and the database are separate systems, so the pair is not atomic.

questions.q: Which is the correct order of work for an outbox?
questions.hint: What is written first, and who sends to the broker?

options.text: Commit the order, then the service publishes to the broker directly, then logs to the outbox
options.why: This has the same gap as before; the outbox saves nothing here.

options.text: Order and outbox row in one transaction, then the relay takes the row and publishes, then marks it sent
options.why: The write is atomic and sending is a separate job. After a crash the row is still unsent, so the relay sends it again.

options.text: The relay publishes first, then the order is saved
options.why: If saving the order fails, an event goes out for an order that doesn't exist.

options.text: The outbox and the order in two separate transactions, then publish
options.why: Separate transactions leave a gap in between, which is exactly what the outbox is meant to avoid.

questions.q: In the code below, the relay crashes after the dispatch but before setting `sent_at`. What happens next?
questions.hint: If sent_at isn't set, what will the relay think of the row next time?

options.text: The row stays unsent, the relay sends it again, and the consumer sees a duplicate
options.why: This is the price of at-least-once, and the reason the consumer needs an inbox.

options.text: The event is lost for good
options.why: It would be lost without an outbox. Here the row is still in the table.

options.text: The order rolls back
options.why: The order was committed long ago; a relay failure doesn't touch it.

questions.q: You add an inbox to the stock handler. Which of these behaviors are correct?
questions.hint: Which transaction holds the inbox write and the stock change?

options.text: The inbox insert and the stock reservation are in the same transaction
options.why: If the work fails, the inbox row rolls back too, so a retry can do the work again.

options.text: A unique constraint on `(message_id, handler)`
options.why: The same message can't be inserted a second time for this handler, and 0 affected rows tells you it's a duplicate.

options.text: Commit the insert first, then reserve stock
options.why: If you crash in between, the message counts as "done" but the stock was never reduced.

options.text: On a duplicate, throw an exception so Messenger retries
options.why: That only causes pointless retries, and the message ends up in the failure queue. Returning quietly is correct.

questions.q: Ryan says: "We have an outbox, so the consumer doesn't need idempotency any more." Is he right?
questions.hint: Which delivery guarantee does an outbox give?

options.text: Yes, an outbox gives exactly-once
options.why: An outbox is at-least-once, not exactly-once.

options.text: No, if the relay crashes an event can go out twice, so the consumer must handle duplicates
options.why: An outbox prevents loss, not duplicates. You need both an outbox and an inbox.

options.text: No, because an outbox never sends the event at all
options.why: An outbox does send the event; the question is how many times.

questions.q: Kevin deletes inbox rows after 1 hour, but the broker can redeliver a message up to 3 days late. What can go wrong?
questions.hint: What does the inbox look for when a late duplicate arrives?

options.text: The inbox insert starts failing forevery message
options.why: Deleting old rows makes inserts easier, not harder.

options.text: Messages are lost, because the inbox swallows them
options.why: The inbox never drops a first delivery. The risk is on duplicates, not on loss.

options.text: A duplicate arriving after 1 hour finds no row, looks new, and does its work again
options.why: The inbox only remembers what is still in the table. Keep rows longer than the longest possible redelivery.

options.text: The relay stops publishing
options.why: The relay works on the outbox, not the inbox.

questions.q: The order service succeeded in payment and stock but failed at the courier service. Why isn't one `ROLLBACK` enough?
questions.hint: Is every service's database the same one?

options.text: Each service already committed in its own database, so it can't be rolled back from outside
options.why: Work that has committed needs a new opposite action (a compensation) to undo it.

options.text: ROLLBACK only works for SELECT
options.why: ROLLBACK does undo writes, but only inside the same transaction.

options.text: Messenger doesn't support rollback
options.why: The problem isn't Messenger; the work was committed in separate services' separate databases.

options.text: The courier service is always slow
options.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

questions.q: Which compensation order is right for this saga? Steps: 1) payment, 2) hold stock, 3) courier (failed).
questions.hint: Should the thing done last be undone first?

options.text: Refund the money, then release the stock
options.why: This order is forward, not reversed: the earlier step is undone first.

options.text: Release the stock, then refund the money
options.why: The last successful step (stock) first and the first step (payment) last: reverse order.

options.text: Both at the same time; order doesn't matter
options.why: Steps may depend on each other, so the order matters.

options.text: Do nothing, the courier will try again
options.why: A retry may be an option, but once the failure is final, compensation is needed.

questions.q: Here is the orchestrator code. Which line stops a duplicate event?
questions.hint: If PaymentCharged arrives a second time, which step will the saga be at?

options.text: `if ('started' !== $saga->step())`: the step has already moved on, so it returns
options.why: On the second arrival the step is no longer started, so ReserveStock isn't sent twice.

options.text: `$this->em->flush()`
options.why: flush only saves the state; it doesn't recognize duplicates.

options.text: `$this->bus->dispatch(...)`
options.why: dispatch sends the next command; it doesn't stop duplicates.

options.text: `#[AsMessageHandler]`
options.why: This attribute only registers the method as a handler.

questions.q: A small flow of two or three steps, and a ten-step flow with conditions: which style fits which?
questions.hint: When does seeing the whole picture in one place matter more?

options.text: Choreography is fine for the small flow; orchestration is better for the big flow with conditions
options.why: As steps grow, the web of events is hard to follow, and timeouts and conditions are easier to handle in one place.

options.text: Choreography for both, because it has less coupling
options.why: Coupling is lower, but the flow is scattered, and finding bugs in a big flow is hard.

options.text: Orchestration for both, because it is the only correct one
options.why: For a small flow an orchestrator can be extra weight. Both are valid; it comes down to complexity.

options.text: Neither needs a saga
options.why: For work across several services, a saga is the usual approach.

questions.q: Which of these saga rules are correct?
questions.hint: What can and can't you do with a failed compensation?

options.text: Compensations must be idempotent
options.why: They must give the same result even when run twice on a retry, for example the same key on a refund.

options.text: Steps that can't be undone (like sending an email) belong at the very end
options.why: If the irreversible action happens only after every earlier step has succeeded, there is less to undo.

options.text: If a compensation fails, you can close the saga as successful
options.why: The customer's money would stay taken. Compensations are retried, not abandoned.

options.text: Keeping the saga's step in memory is enough
options.why: A restart loses everything. The step must be kept in the database.

questions.q: The saga waits for the courier and times out at minute 5. At minute 6 the courier service books a van, but its reply is lost. What should the saga do at minute 5?
questions.hint: The timeout told you nothing about whether the booking exists.

options.text: Cancel the courier booking by its key, then release stock and refund
options.why: The step's outcome is unknown, so it is undone too. The cancel works whether or not the booking exists, and a late booking is refused.

options.text: Release stock and refund only, because the courier step failed
options.why: It didn't necessarily fail. If the van gets booked at minute 6, a courier arrives for a dead order.

options.text: Wait until the courier answers, however long that takes
options.why: The saga hangs forever and the customer's money stays taken. The deadline exists to stop that.

options.text: Send a new BookCourier with a fresh key and hope one succeeds
options.why: If the first booking worked, you now have two vans. A retry must reuse the same key.

questions.q: Rachel is owed $30 back from a $120 payment. Which design is right?
questions.hint: History must not be lost, and it must match the gateway.

options.text: Set `payment.amount` to $90
options.why: The original amount is lost, it doesn't match the gateway, and nobody can say why $30 went back.

options.text: Keep the payment unchanged and create a new Refund record for $30, linked to the payment
options.why: History stays intact, and the remaining amount comes from adding up the records.

options.text: Delete the payment and create a new one for $90
options.why: Deleting is even worse: you lose the proof of the original transaction.

options.text: Write "partially_refunded" in the status column and nothing else
options.why: How much went back, when and why is all missing. A status alone isn't enough.

questions.q: From the table below, what is the remaining refundable amount? P-1: +$120, R-1: −$30 (P-1), R-2: −$20 (P-1).
questions.hint: The original minus all the Refunds.

options.why: That is the original amount; the earlier refunds haven't been counted.
You subtracted only the first refund; there is a second one too.
The two refunds add up to $50, but that is what has gone back, not what remains.

questions.q: What is wrong with this refund code?
questions.hint: What if two agents come in at once? And what if the request is retried?

options.text: No lock: two agents can see the same remaining amount and both get approved
options.why: There is a gap between the read and the write. Without PESSIMISTIC_WRITE or a unique constraint, over-refunding is possible.

options.text: No idempotency key: a retry will create the same refund twice
options.why: It creates a new Refund every time, because there is no way to recognize the earlier request.

options.text: Creating a new Refund record is wrong; it should change a payment column
options.why: A new record is the right approach. The problems are the missing lock and key.

options.text: It shouldn't persist; flush alone is enough
options.why: A new entity always needs persist; that isn't the problem.

questions.q: From Rachel's $120 authorization, $80 was captured with the first shipment. Then the third item was canceled. Which is the correct record for the remaining $40?
questions.hint: Was that $40 ever taken from the customer's card?

options.text: A Refund of $40
options.why: A refund applies once the money has been taken. Here the $40 was only held.

options.text: A Void of $40, against the authorization
options.why: Releasing money that is held but not taken is a void (reversal).

options.text: Change the authorization amount to $80
options.why: You never change the original record. The remaining share gets a new Void record.

options.text: Do nothing; it will release itself when it expires
options.why: The customer's money stays held until it expires. Voiding directly is the right move.

questions.q: Which practices keep fee rules safe and easy to change?
questions.hint: When a rule changes, how much code and arithmetic must you touch?

options.text: Keep the rules in a database table staff can edit, such as a `days > 7` condition and a bp value
options.why: A rule change is one updated row, with no deploy.

options.text: Calculate in integers: `intdiv($amount * $bp, 10_000)`
options.why: No float noise, and the result is the same every time.

options.text: Drop the fee and just write a smaller Refund amount
options.why: Then the Refund won't match the gateway, and you lose how much fee was taken. The fee is a separate record.

options.text: Hard-code `$fee = $amount * 0.1` in the code
options.why: Floats make the cents drift, and changing a rule means changing code.

options.text: List the rules in `services.yaml`, so changing them needs no deploy
options.why: That file ships with the code, so editing it is a deploy. Only a table (or similar store) changes at runtime.

questions.q: In which situation does event sourcing make the most sense?
questions.hint: Where is "how did we get here?" the central question?

options.text: Storing a user's profile photo and name
options.why: Only the current value matters here; history isn't a main requirement. Plain CRUD is enough.

options.text: A bank ledger, where every transaction needs its history and reasons for audit
options.why: The sequence of events is the real data here, and the balance is its result.

options.text: The comment count on a blog
options.why: Incrementing and decrementing a number is enough; no history is needed.

options.text: A site's dark mode setting
options.why: One current value, and no history needed.

questions.q: In the event store below, what stops two concurrent writers from getting the same version for two events?
questions.code:
CREATE TABLE event_store (
  aggregate_id uuid        NOT NULL,
  version      int         NOT NULL,
  type         varchar(80) NOT NULL,
  payload      jsonb       NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (aggregate_id, version)
);
questions.hint: Can two rows go in with the same primary key?

options.text: The (aggregate_id, version) primary key doesn't allow a second row with the same pair
options.why: The database itself stops one writer, who gets a ConcurrentModification.

options.text: A `jsonb` column doesn't store the same value twice
options.why: It has nothing to do with the payload.

options.text: The `uuid` type increments the version automatically
options.why: A uuid is just an identity; incrementing the version is our code's job.

options.text: Nothing stops it, and both rows will be stored
options.why: The primary key stops exactly that.

questions.q: Which statements about `fromHistory()` and `withdraw()` on the Account aggregate are correct?
questions.hint: Are the rules applied to past events?

options.text: `fromHistory()` replays past events to build state and enforces no rules
options.why: The events have already happened, so there is nothing to validate again.

options.text: `withdraw()` checks the balance rule and puts a new event into pending
options.why: The rules apply to a new command, and the event is born as its result.

options.text: `fromHistory()` writes new events straight to the database
options.why: It only builds state. Writing is done by EventStore::append().

options.text: `withdraw()` runs an UPDATE on a balance column in the database
options.why: Event sourcing doesn't update a balance column; it appends an event.

questions.q: Rachel withdraws money, looks at her balance straight away and still sees the old value. What is the most accurate explanation?
questions.hint: When does the projection update?

options.text: The write to the event store failed
options.why: The write succeeded; the read model just hasn't caught up yet.

options.text: The read model is updated slightly later by the projector, which is eventual consistency
options.why: Writing and reading use separate models, so there is a small gap in between.

options.text: The event store gave wrong data
options.why: The source of truth, the event store, is right; the read copy is behind.

options.text: It's a bug; a projection should never lag
options.why: Lag is the normal price of this design. You handle it in the UI with the version, or by waiting.

questions.q: The projector has the condition `WHERE account_balance.version = :v - 1`. What is its benefit?
questions.hint: What happens if an event arrives twice or out of order?

options.text: It prevents wrong updates when an event is a duplicate or an earlier one hasn't arrived yet
options.why: The balance changes only when this is exactly the next version, so the projector is safe and idempotent.

options.text: The query runs faster
options.why: It isn't about speed; it is a correctness condition.

options.text: It changes the order of versions in the event store
options.why: The event store isn't touched here; the condition applies to the read model.

questions.q: `MoneyDeposited` used to carry only `amount`, and now `currency` is mandatory. Thousands of old events are in the database. What is the right approach?
questions.hint: Can an event be changed?

options.text: UPDATE all the old events to add `currency`
options.why: Events are immutable; changing them rewrites history and ruins their value for audit.

options.text: Delete the old events and write them again in the new shape
options.why: Deleting is even worse: the history is gone.

options.text: Let an upcaster convert old schema_v events to the new shape when they are read
options.why: The original events stay intact in the database, and the code always receives the latest shape.

options.text: Build a separate Account table for the new shape and drop the old one
options.why: You would lose the old history, and the state would be split up wrongly.

questions.q: Ryan changes `apply()` so that withdrawals now include a fee. Old snapshots of the balance exist. What should he do?
questions.hint: Which is the truth: the snapshot or the events?

options.text: Keep the snapshots: they are the source of truth
options.why: The events are the truth. A snapshot is only a saved result of the old rules.

options.text: Delete the snapshots and let them be rebuilt from the events with the new rules
options.why: Old snapshots hold balances computed by the old rules. Rebuilding from the events gives the right ones.

options.text: Delete the oldest events to match the snapshots
options.why: Never delete events. That destroys the history that everything else is built from.

options.text: Edit each snapshot by hand to subtract the fees
options.why: Hand edits are error-prone, and the events can rebuild every snapshot automatically.
